target: AG1’s claim that Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway show renewable replacement is broadly achievable
objection: Those very high alternative-energy shares are atypical one-off cases: they depend on unusual local resource endowments and relatively constrained system contexts, so they should not be treated as a generally replicable template for replacing fossil fuels in typical large countries.

target: AG1’s implication that high renewable shares in those countries show alternatives can replace fossil fuels in general
objection: High alternative-energy shares in a few electricity systems do not generalize to most places at the scale required to replace fossil fuels as a primary energy source in large countries.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that alternatives can replace fossil fuels without a fossil bridge
objection: Large electric grids need reliable, dispatchable energy, and the historical fact that U.S. alternative energy use has never exceeded 20% is cited as evidence that alternatives have not supplied enough firm capacity to remove fossil fuels as the baseline energy source.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energies can effectively replace fossil fuels
objection: Because the cited high-renewable cases are not broadly replicable and alternatives have not shown they can fully remove fossil fuels under real reliability constraints, effective replacement requires a bridge fuel such as natural gas rather than relying on alternative energies alone.

target: AG1’s use of the Iceland/Paraguay/Costa Rica/Norway examples as evidence that they are replicable beyond special cases
objection: Those countries’ very high alternative-energy shares reflect a generally replicable energy-system buildout capability rather than mere one-off anomalies, so the ‘not replicable’ criticism is unwarranted.

target: AG1’s reliance on electricity-system renewables examples as proof of fossil-fuel replacement
objection: Very high shares of alternative energy in national electricity systems do not by themselves show that fossil fuels are replaced across the whole economy, because major fossil-fuel uses like transport and industrial heat remain outside electricity generation.

target: AG1’s claim that scaling alternative electricity is enough for effective fossil-fuel replacement
objection: Scaling alternative electricity alone does not automatically decarbonize transport and industrial-heat uses, so electricity growth by itself cannot establish effective overall replacement of fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s conclusion that the evidence warrants saying alternatives can replace fossil fuels
objection: Because the supporting evidence addresses only electricity shares and not major non-electricity fossil uses, it does not justify the claim that alternative energies effectively replace fossil fuels overall.

target: AG1’s claim that low-carbon electricity plus electrification can replace fossil fuels
objection: That argument depends on nuclear being able to supply a meaningful share of reliable low-carbon electricity at the scale needed for electrification, so its success hinges on nuclear being viable.

target: AG1’s reliance on nuclear as part of the replacement pathway
objection: Nuclear energy is too dangerous and ineffective to be a serious solution to global warming, because accidents like Fukushima can erase the carbon-free electricity gains through severe harmful outcomes.

target: AG1’s assumption that nuclear can reliably backstop renewables for electrification
objection: If nuclear cannot be relied on to provide the needed reliable low-carbon electricity, then renewables alone cannot supply the reliability needed to support full fossil-fuel replacement via electrification.

target: AG1’s conclusion that alternatives can replace fossil fuels using renewables plus nuclear
objection: Because the replacement strategy depends on nuclear, and nuclear is not a reliable, safe way to provide the required low-carbon electricity, alternative energies cannot provide the basis for fully replacing fossil fuels.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can replace fossil fuels without a natural-gas bridge
objection: If electrification still leaves fossil-fuel uses such as chemical feedstocks and some high energy-density needs unmet, then alternative electricity does not eliminate all major categories of fossil-fuel use and cannot by itself replace fossil fuels as the overall energy basis.

target: AG1’s claim that a renewables-plus-nuclear strategy makes natural gas unnecessary
objection: Because full fossil-fuel replacement cannot be achieved by alternative electricity and electrification alone, decarbonization still requires a dispatchable fossil bridge during the transition, with natural gas serving that role.

target: AG1’s reliance on a low U.S. historical alternative-energy share being irrelevant
objection: To replace fossil fuels as the energy basis in large countries, alternatives must supply the dominant share of total energy demand, not merely a large share of electricity in limited cases; the U.S. figure shows they have not demonstrated that dominance.

target: AG1’s claim that natural gas is not a necessary bridge
objection: If alternatives have not demonstrated dominance as the energy basis in large countries, then effective replacement still requires some fossil-fuel role during the transition, making a fossil bridge like natural gas necessary.

target: AG1’s claim that continued fossil use during the transition only affects timing
objection: Because end-use equipment like vehicles, industrial burners, and building heat systems lasts a long time, effective replacement requires low-carbon energy to remain sufficient and reliable throughout the long transition, not just briefly.

target: AG1’s confidence that renewables plus nuclear can provide the needed transition power
objection: Renewables are variable and nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective to be relied on as a safe, dependable, quickly scalable firm low-carbon source, so alternatives cannot be counted on to provide sustained firm carbon-free power across the transition period.

target: AG1’s conclusion that alternatives can fully replace fossil fuels during the transition
objection: If alternatives cannot reliably provide sustained firm carbon-free power across the long period needed for full fossil displacement, then fossil fuels must continue to supply substantial baseline and backup energy, meaning they have not been effectively replaced.

target: AG1’s claim that natural gas is not a necessary prerequisite for replacement
objection: Because alternatives cannot fully replace fossil fuels under these reliability and safety constraints, a dispatchable fossil bridge such as natural gas is needed during the transition.

target: AG1’s claim that renewables can meet reliability needs without fossil fuels as a prerequisite bridge
objection: Renewables are variable, and there is no dependable, quickly scalable carbon-free firm alternative to provide the dispatchable reliability needed while scaling, so fossil fuels must remain the standing provider of reliable dispatchable energy.

target: AG1’s claim that continued fossil use during the transition does not prevent effective replacement
objection: Because long-lived end-use equipment means low-carbon power must be sustained over long periods, continued fossil use implies effective overall replacement is not yet achieved if firm low-carbon supply cannot be maintained.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can provide firm carbon-free power via renewables plus nuclear
objection: Alternatives cannot be relied on to provide sustained firm, carbon-free electricity over the long period needed for full fossil displacement, because renewables are variable and nuclear is unsafe and ineffective as a serious solution.

target: AG1’s claim that continued fossil use does not mean fossil fuels remain structurally necessary
objection: If alternatives cannot reliably provide sustained firm low-carbon power across the transition, then fossil fuels must continue to play a substantial baseline role, so they have not been effectively replaced as the energy basis.

target: AG1’s claim that non-fossil firming, storage, transmission, and demand response can replace fossil balancing
objection: The reliability need during periods when renewables underperform can only be met by keeping fossil fuels, such as natural gas, as an essential dispatch backbone; non-fossil firming is not the only necessary solution.

target: AG1’s claim that high-share renewable systems prove long-run reliability without fossil fuels
objection: Even if some countries have very high renewable electricity shares, the controlled renewable and dispatchable resources cited are not enough to prove that renewables alone can guarantee sufficient firm, dispatchable energy over long periods.

target: AG1’s use of the U.S. historical alternative-energy share as irrelevant
objection: A country’s historical overall alternative-energy share is not the measure of grid reliability; effective replacement requires firm, dispatchable low-carbon capacity and system flexibility, which the low U.S. share indicates have not been demonstrated at scale.

target: AG1’s claim that controllable renewables and grid flexibility can support replacement
objection: Controllable renewables like reservoir-managed hydropower and geothermal are geographically constrained and limited by site availability, so they cannot be assumed to scale enough in many large fossil-reliant countries to provide the needed firm capacity.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can eliminate the fossil baseline role in large systems
objection: If controllable renewables cannot be assumed to provide sufficient firm dispatchable capacity at large scale, then alternatives cannot reliably replace fossil fuels as the energy basis in real large systems.

target: AG1’s claim that natural gas is not a required bridge
objection: When reliable firm low-carbon alternatives cannot fully replace fossil baseline power immediately, a fossil bridge is needed; natural gas is dispatchable and uses existing infrastructure to cut emissions rapidly while alternatives scale up.
